'''John Robert Huizenga''' (April 21, 1921 – January 25, 2014) was an American [[physicist]] who helped build the first [[atomic bomb]] and who also debunked [[University of Utah]] scientists' claim of achieving [[cold fusion]].<ref name=NYTBio>{{cite news|title=John R. Huizenga, Physicist at Fore of Nuclear Era, Dies at 92|work=New York Times|author=William J. Broad|date=January 29, 2014|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/01/30/science/john-r-huizenga-physicist-at-fore-of-nuclear-era-dies-at-92.html}}</ref><ref name=UoRObit>{{cite web|title=Professor Emeritus John R. Huizenga, a Key Figure in the 1989 National Review of Cold Fusion Claims, Dies at Age 92|publisher=University of Rochester|date=January 29, 2014|accessdate=January 30, 2014|url=http://www.rochester.edu/news/show.php?id=8222}}</ref><ref name=UoRDoC>{{cite web|title=Department of Chemistry|publisher=University of Rochester|location=Rochester, N.Y.|accessdate=April 27, 2014|url=http://www.chem.rochester.edu/faculty/faculty.php?name=huizenga}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
John Robert Huizenga was born on a farm near [[Fulton, Illinois]], the son of Henry and Josie (Brands) Huizenga.<ref name=ClintonObit/>  He attended [[Erie High School (Illinois)|Erie High School]] and [[Morrison High School (Illinois)|Morrison High School]], graduating from the latter in 1940.  He continued his education at [[Calvin College]] in Michigan, from which he received a bachelor's degree in 1944.  He would maintain his ties to Calvin later in life, for example collaborating on fundamental nuclear research with his Calvin friend [[Roger Griffioen]],<ref name=GriffPaper>For example, {{cite journal | last1=Griffioen | first1=R.D. | last2=Thompson | first2=R.C. | last3=Huizenga | first3=J.R. | title=Levels of 235Np excited by the 234U(3He, d) and 234U(alpha, t) reactions | journal=Physical Review C | volume=18 | issue=2 | year=1978 | pages=671–678|bibcode = 1978PhRvC..18..671G |doi = 10.1103/PhysRevC.18.671 }}</ref> who had gone on to become a professor there.  Calvin would name him one of the college's Distinguished Alumni in 1975.<ref name=CC-alum>{{cite web | url=http://www.calvin.edu/alumni/about/awards/daa_recipients.htm | title=Calvin Alumni Association Awards: Distinguished Alumni Award: Past Recipients | publisher=Calvin College Alumni Association | accessdate=12 May 2014}}</ref>

Along with other Calvin students, he was recruited after graduation to work for the [[Manhattan Project]], at the Project's site in [[Oak Ridge, Tennessee]], that was dedicated to the production of [[Enriched uranium#Highly enriched uranium (HEU)|highly enriched uranium]].  Following his time in Oak Ridge, he continued his education at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign|University of Illinois]], receiving a Doctor of Philosophy degree in physical chemistry in 1949. On completing his studies he held joint appointments at the [[University of Chicago]] and [[Argonne National Laboratory]].<ref name=UoRObit/>

==Professional career==
During World War II, Huizenga supervised teams at the [[Manhattan Project]] in Oak Ridge, Tenn., involved in enriching uranium used in the atomic weapon dropped on Hiroshima in August 1945. During his Argonne years, as a result of examining debris from the "[[Ivy Mike]]" [[Nuclear weapons testing|nuclear test]] in 1952, Huizenga was part of the team that added two new [[Synthetic element|synthetic chemical elements]], [[einsteinium]] and [[fermium]], to the [[periodic table]].<ref name=NYTBio/><ref name=UoRObit/><ref name = "ES_FM">{{cite journal | last1=Ghiorso | author-link=Albert Ghiorso | first1=A. | last2=Thompson | first2=S. | last3=Higgins | first3=G. | last4=Seaborg | author4-link=Glenn T. Seaborg | first4=G. | last5=Studier | first5=M. | last6=Fields | first6=P. | last7=Fried | first7=S. | last8=Diamond | first8=H. | last9=Mech | first9=J. | first10=G. | last10=Pyle | first11=J. | last11=Huizenga | first12=A. | last12=Hirsch | first13=W. | last13=Manning | first14=C. | last14=Browne | first15=H. | last15=Smith | first16=R. | last16=Spence | title=New Elements Einsteinium and Fermium, Atomic Numbers 99 and 100 | journal=Phys. Rev. | volume=99 | issue=3 | url=http://escholarship.org/uc/item/70q401ct | doi=10.1103/PhysRev.99.1048 | pages=1048–1049 | year=1955 | bibcode=1955PhRv...99.1048G| doi-access=free }} [https://books.google.com/books?id=e53sNAOXrdMC&pg=PA91 Google Books]</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Fields | first1=P. | last2=Studier | first2=M. | last3=Diamond | first3=H. | last4=Mech | first4=J. | last5=Inghram | first5=M. | last6=Pyle | first6=G. | last7=Stevens | first7=C. | last8=Fried | first8=S. | last9=Manning | first9=W. | first10=G. | last10=Pyle | first11=J. | last11=Huizenga | first12=A. | last12=Hirsch | first13=W. | last13=Manning | first14=C. | last14=Browne | first15=H. | last15=Smith | first16=R. | last16=Spence | title=Transplutonium Elements in Thermonuclear Test Debris | journal=Physical Review | volume=102 | issue=1 | year=1956 | pages=180–182 | doi=10.1103/PhysRev.102.180 | bibcode=1956PhRv..102..180F}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=e53sNAOXrdMC&pg=PA93 Google Books]</ref>  Huizenga and his colleagues were at first unable to publish papers on their discoveries in the open literature, because of classification concerns relating to the nuclear test,<ref name="Ghiorso-C&EN">{{cite journal | first=Albert | last=Ghiorso | author-link=Albert Ghiorso | year=2003  | title=Einsteinium and Fermium | journal=Chemical and Engineering News | url=http://pubs.acs.org/cen/80th/einsteiniumfermium.html | volume=81 | issue=36 | doi=10.1021/cen-v081n036.p174 | pages=174–175| url-access=subscription }}</ref> but these concerns were eventually resolved, and the team was able to publish in ''[[Physical Review]]'' and thus claim priority for their discovery.  During his Argonne years he was one of the founders of the [[Gordon Research Conferences]] on [[nuclear chemistry]], serving as chairman of the nuclear chemistry Gordon Conference in 1958.<ref name="GordConf">{{cite web | url=http://www.grc.org/conferences.aspx?id=0000181 | title=Conference Portfolio: Nuclear Chemistry | date= 2014 | publisher=Gordon Research Conferences | accessdate= 30 April 2014}}</ref> He received a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] in 1964 and took a sabbatical from Argonne to further his studies as a visiting professor at the [[University of Paris]] for the 1964–1965 academic year.

In 1967, he became a professor of chemistry and physics at the [[University of Rochester]] where he worked for the remainder of his career, apart from a second Guggenheim Fellowship that allowed him to engage in research during the 1973–1974 school year at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], the [[Technical University of Munich]], and the [[Niels Bohr Institute]] in [[Copenhagen]].  His research interests at Rochester covered topics in [[nuclear structure]] of [[actinide]]s, [[nuclear fission]], and [[nuclear reaction]]s between heavy ions.  He was chairman of the Department of Chemistry from 1983 to 1988,<ref name=UoRChemHist>{{cite web | url=http://www.chem.rochester.edu/about/resources/history.pdf | title=Chemistry at Rochester: 75th Anniversary of Graduate Education | editor=Debra Haring | date=October 2007 | publisher=The University of Rochester Chemistry Department | accessdate=29 April 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130721090834/http://www.chem.rochester.edu/about/resources/history.pdf | archive-date=21 July 2013 | url-status=dead }}</ref> retiring as Tracy H. Harris Professor (later Professor Emeritus) of Chemistry.

During Huizenga's time at Rochester, the university had its own [[particle accelerator]], a [[Van de Graaff generator|tandem Van de Graaff accelerator]] that produced beams of nuclei accelerated to energies of several [[Electronvolt|MeV]] per nucleon.  This facility, which opened in 1966,<ref name="Gove">{{cite book |last= Gove |first= Harry E. |date= 1998|title= From Hiroshima to the Iceman: The Development and Applications of Accelerator Mass Spectrometry|publisher= CRC Press|page= 4|isbn= 978-0750305587}}</ref> afforded him the opportunity to continue his research program in experimental nuclear science.  However, the limited beam energies available led him to more powerful accelerators, such as the [[SuperHILAC]] at Berkeley and the [[Los Alamos Neutron Science Center|Los Alamos Meson Physics Facility]], LAMPF, at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]], for his experimental work.  His LAMPF proposal to study actinide [[Exotic atom|muonic atom]]s was one of the earliest experiments to receive beam time at the LAMPF stopped-muon facility.<ref name="MWJ-muons">{{cite journal | last=Johnson | first=M.W. | last2=Schröder | first2=W.U. | last3=Huizenga | first3=J.R. | last4=Hensley | first4=W.K. | last5=Perry | first5=D.G. | last6=Browne | author6-link=John C. Browne | first6=J.C. | date=1977 | title=Measurement of total muon-capture rates in Th232, U235,238, and Pu239 | journal=Physical Review | volume=C 15 | issue=6 | pages=2169–2173 | doi=10.1103/physrevc.15.2169 |bibcode = 1977PhRvC..15.2169J }}</ref>

In 1989, Huizenga co-chaired, with [[Norman Foster Ramsey, Jr.|Norman Ramsey]], a panel convened by the [[United States Department of Energy]] which attempted to debunk claims by two University of Utah chemists that they had achieved [[Cold fusion|nuclear fusion at room temperature]].  The findings of the Huizenga/Ramsey panel, although highly skeptical of the reality of cold fusion, were cautious:

<blockquote>Based on the examination of published reports, reprints, numerous communications to the Panel and several site visits, the Panel concludes that the experimental results of excess heat from calorimetric cells reported to date do not present convincing evidence that useful sources of energy will result from the phenomena attributed to cold fusion. ...&nbsp;The Panel concludes that the experiments reported to date do not present convincing evidence to associate the reported anomalous heat with a nuclear process.&nbsp;...

Current understanding of the very extensive literature of experimental and theoretical results for hydrogen in solids gives no support for the occurrence of cold fusion in solids. Specifically, no theoretical or experimental evidence suggests the existence of D-D distances shorter than that in the molecule D2 or the achievement of "confinement" pressure above relatively modest levels. The known behavior of deuterium in solids does not give any support for the supposition that the fusion probability is enhanced by the presence of the palladium, titanium, or other elements.

Nuclear fusion at room temperature, of the type discussed in this report, would be contrary to all understanding gained of nuclear reactions in the last half century; it would require the invention of an entirely new nuclear process.<ref name="ERAB-summary">{{cite web | url=http://files.ncas.org/erab/execsumm.htm | title=Executive Summary of the Energy Resources Advisory Board's Cold Fusion Panel | date=26 November 1989 | accessdate=12 May 2014}}</ref></blockquote>

However, Huizenga later published a book titled "Cold Fusion: The Scientific Fiasco of the Century".<ref name=NYTBio/><ref name=UoRObit/>

==Awards and honors==
[[File:HD.3F.024 (11086559596) (cropped).jpg|alt=Photo of Huizenga being awarded the Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award bestowed by Glenn T. Seaborg.|thumb|Huizenga (left) being awarded the [[Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award]] by [[Glenn T. Seaborg]] in 1966]]
Huizenga was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1976 and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (Fellow) in 1992.  He was a 1966 recipient of the [[Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award]] bestowed by the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission]].

==Personal life==
Huizenga married Dorothy Koeze in 1946.<ref name=ClintonObit>{{cite news|title=The life journey of Whiteside County native, John R. Huizenga|work=The Clinton Herald|date=February 7, 2014|accessdate=April 27, 2014|url=http://www.clintonherald.com/topnews/x1782781644/The-life-journey-of-Whiteside-County-native-John-R-Huizenga/print}}</ref> They had two sons and two daughters. One son, Dr. [[Robert Huizenga]], is a prominent physician whose career has included a stint as [[team physician]] for the [[Oakland Raiders#Los Angeles era (1982–1994)|Los Angeles Raiders]] American football team.

Following his retirement from Rochester, Huizenga and his wife moved to [[North Carolina]], where he continued to serve on advisory committees at major accelerator laboratories, worked to debunk cold fusion, and wrote his memoirs. Dolly Huizenga died in 1999. John Huizenga died of [[heart failure]] in [[San Diego, California]], in January 2014, aged 92.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Iglinski |first=Peter |last2= |first2= |date=2014-01-30 |title=John R. Huizenga, pioneer in nuclear science, dies at 92 |url=https://www.rochester.edu/newscenter/john-r-huizenga-pioneer-in-nuclear-science-dies-at-92/ |access-date=2025-10-04 |website=News Center |language=en-US}}</ref>
